notes.meaning: Anyone who sells a home inside a walled city has one full year to buy it back. This rule gave families time to recover from a sudden crisis without losing their house right away. Unlike open farmland, city houses were built by human hands and were not part of the original family land given by God.

If the owner cannot buy the city home back within twelve months, the buyer owns it permanently. The house does not return to the original family during the Jubilee year. This rule gave lasting security to buyers and encouraged traders and newcomers to settle in the cities.

Houses in villages without walls follow the same rules as open farmland. Because these homes were tied directly to farming the surrounding soil, the original owner could buy them back at any time. If they were not bought back earlier, they went back to the original family freely in the Year of Jubilee.

The Levites received a special rule for the houses in the cities assigned to them across the land. Since the tribe of Levi had no large territory of farmland, their city homes counted as their primary inheritance. Because of this, a Levite always kept the right to buy back his house at any time.

If another person buys a house from a Levite, that house must return to the Levite in the Year of Jubilee. God set this rule to protect the tribe that served at His sanctuary from losing their shelter. These city homes were their only tribal share among the people of Israel.

The open grazing fields surrounding the Levitical towns could never be sold under any circumstances. These lands belonged in common to all the Levites of that town to feed their livestock. Selling them would permanently destroy the food supply God provided for their daily needs.

When a fellow countryman falls into poverty and cannot support himself, his neighbors must step in and help him. God commands the community to sustain him with food and shelter just as they would care for a resident foreigner. God calls His people to show mercy and keep a struggling brother from losing his livelihood.

An Israelite was forbidden to charge interest or make a profit when helping a needy neighbor. Taking advantage of someone in hard times goes against the holy respect God expects His people to have for Him. Revering God means treating a struggling brother with kindness so that he can survive.

God makes the command specific by forbidding both money lent at interest and food sold for a profit to the poor. Loans to needy brothers were meant as acts of charity, not business deals to make extra money. God's people were expected to share what they had to help others get back on their feet.

The LORD reminds Israel that He rescued them from slavery in Egypt to give them Canaan and to be their God. Because the Israelites had received God's free mercy and rescue, they were expected to pass that mercy on to others. True generosity to the poor flows out of remembering what God has already done.

If an Israelite becomes so poor that he must sell his labor to a neighbor to survive, the buyer must not treat him like a slave. He was not to be forced into humiliating or crushing slave work. Even in deep poverty, a child of God was still a brother who deserved respect.

The poor brother was to be treated like a hired worker or a resident guest who receives fair wages. He would work for his employer only until the Year of Jubilee arrived. This rule guaranteed that working off a debt was always temporary and humane.

When the Year of Jubilee arrived, the worker and his children were set completely free. He was allowed to return to his extended family and take back his inherited land. God designed the Jubilee so that no family in Israel would remain stuck in poverty forever.

God explains that the people of Israel are His personal servants because He bought them out of Egyptian slavery. Since God holds the first claim on their lives, no human owner has the right to treat them as personal property. They could never be sold in a public market like ordinary goods.

Employers were forbidden to treat their Hebrew workers with cruelty, harsh words, or unreasonable tasks. The command to fear God reminded masters that the Lord watches how they treat those under their authority. Living with reverence for God means treating every worker with fairness and care.

Israel was permitted to buy long-term male and female servants from the surrounding foreign nations. Unlike fellow Israelites, these foreign workers were not released automatically at the Jubilee. This allowed households to find necessary help while preserving special protections for covenant brothers.

Israelites could also purchase servants from the foreign families living inside the land of Israel. Children born to those resident foreigners could also become household servants. These workers became a lasting part of the family household that bought them.

Foreign servants could be passed down as an inheritance to a man's children as permanent possessions. In contrast, God repeated the rule that Israelites must never rule harshly over their fellow countrymen. This difference reminded Israel that all members of God's covenant were brothers who belonged to the Lord.

A foreigner living in Israel might become wealthy, while an Israelite living near him might fall into deep poverty. In desperation, the poor Israelite might sell his service to that prosperous foreigner or someone in his clan. Even in that situation, God provided a way to keep the poor man from being lost to his people.

An Israelite who sold himself to a foreigner kept the legal right to be bought back at any time. One of his brothers had the opportunity and family duty to step forward and pay for his freedom. This rule protected God's people from remaining under foreign control.

Any close relative, like an uncle or a cousin, was allowed to pay the redemption price for the poor man. If the man later earned enough money himself, he was fully permitted to buy his own freedom. God designed family loyalty as a practical shield for the poor and vulnerable.

To find the right cost to buy him back, the servant and his foreign owner counted the years left until the Jubilee. The price was calculated fairly by matching those remaining years against the standard yearly wage of a hired worker. This prevented the master from being cheated while keeping the price fair for the servant.

If many years remained until the next Jubilee, the servant or his relative had to pay back a larger share of the original price. The cost depended directly on how much labor was still owed under the agreement. This protected the foreign buyer from losing the work he had already paid for.

If only a few years remained before the Year of Jubilee, the price to buy the man's freedom was small. The redeemer paid only for the short time left until the Jubilee would set the servant free anyway. God's law required honest and fair dealing for both sides in the transaction.

The foreign master was required to treat the Hebrew servant like a worker hired from year to year, not like a slave. Fellow Israelites were also commanded not to stand by and watch a foreigner abuse their countryman. The community had a duty to look out for their brother and stop unfair mistreatment.

Even if no relative stepped in to buy him back and he had no money to free himself, the man and his children went free in the Year of Jubilee. Foreign masters living in the land were required to obey this law just like native Israelites. No circumstance could keep a child of Israel in permanent servitude.

God closes the chapter by repeating why this freedom is guaranteed: the people of Israel are His own servants. He delivered them out of Egypt so that they would belong to Him alone. Because the LORD is their God, no human master has the right to claim permanent ownership over them.
